title: Qualifying an Expert Witness: What Actually Establishes Competence
description: Qualification attaches to the specific opinion, not the expert generally. Here's what establishes it and the four gaps that draw challenges.

blocks.text: Qualification is the threshold question, and it is also the one attorneys most often assume is settled because the CV looks impressive.

An expert is qualified by knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education. Any one of those can suffice. What matters is whether the qualification connects to the specific opinion being offered, and that connection is where challenges land.
Qualification Is Opinion-Specific, Not General
The most common misunderstanding is treating qualification as a property of the person rather than of the person-opinion pair.

A board-certified surgeon with thirty years of practice is unquestionably qualified as a surgeon. Whether they are qualified to opine on the standard of care for a particular procedure they have not performed in fifteen years is a separate question, and courts treat it that way.
The test is narrow: does this expert's background specifically support the opinion in this case? Not a related opinion, not the general subject area. This one.
The Four Common Qualification Gaps

Adjacent expertise. The expert practices in a field that touches the issue without covering it. A mechanical engineer opining on an electrical failure. An internist opining on a subspecialty standard of care. The CV reads as relevant and the specific match is missing.

Stale currency. Credentials earned long ago, in a field that has since changed. This matters more in medicine and technology than in disciplines where the fundamentals are stable, but it is always a cross-examination topic.

Academic without practical, or practical without academic. Depending on the opinion, either can be a gap. An academic who has never done the work in the field may struggle on practical standard-of-care questions. A practitioner with no formal training may struggle on methodology questions.

Credential inflation. Certifications from organizations with minimal requirements, memberships presented as credentials, or titles that sound authoritative without meaning much. Opposing counsel will look up every organization on the CV.
What Actually Establishes Qualification
Direct practice in the specific area at issue, ideally current or recent.
Board certification or the field's equivalent, from a recognized body, in the relevant specialty rather than a general one.
Training specific to the methodology the opinion relies on.
Publication or teaching in the area, which is not required but is strong support.
Prior qualification by courts on substantially similar opinions.
Prior qualification is worth particular attention. An expert who has been accepted on this type of opinion before has a track record. One who has been rejected has a problem you need to know about.
Voir Dire of the Expert

Opposing counsel may voir dire your expert on qualifications before they testify. The questioning targets exactly the gaps above: what specifically qualifies you to opine on this, when did you last do this work, what training do you have in this particular method.
Preparation means the expert can answer each of those directly and specifically. Vague answers about general experience are what qualification challenges are built on.
Screening at Retention
Before retaining, get concrete answers to:
What specifically in your background supports this exact opinion?
When did you last practice in this specific area?
What certifications do you hold, from which bodies, and in what specialty?
Have you been qualified by a court on this type of opinion before?
Have you ever been found unqualified or had your qualification limited?
An expert who answers these crisply has thought about their own qualification. One who redirects to general experience has not.
When One Expert Is Not Enough

Qualification problems often trace to trying to cover too much ground with one person. If the case requires opinions in two genuinely different disciplines, one expert stretched across both creates a qualification gap in at least one of them.
Recognizing that early is cheaper than discovering it after disclosure, when the second expert has to be found and prepared on a compressed schedule.

The Bottom Line

Qualification attaches to the opinion, not the person. The failures are adjacent expertise, stale currency, a mismatch between academic and practical background, and credentials that do not hold up to inspection. Screen by asking what specifically supports this exact opinion, and treat a general answer as a warning.
